sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Veles** ​(*veles*) — ‌Cattle, ‌Commerce, Underworld ​· ​Cattle god, ​possibly wool ​— ​belongs to ‌the ​Slavic tradition, ​where ‌it is ​catalogued ‌under the ​domain ‌"Cattle, Commerce, ​Underworld". The ​name ​means "Cattle ​god, ​possibly wool"[^1].

‌**Veles** ​— Volos ‌to ​the East ‌Slavs ​— is ‌the god ​of ‌cattle and ​wealth, ​of the ‌underworld's ‌moist depths, ‌and, ​in the ​great ‌reconstruction of ​Ivanov and ​Toporov, ‌of poetry ​and ​magic. Where ‌Perun ​strikes from ‌above, ​Veles moves ​below: ​through herds, ​graves, bargains, ‌and ‌song.[^2]

PuniCodex ​records ‌the canonical ​scholarly ​spelling **Veles** ‌and ‌serves its ‌temple ‌at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/veles/). The ‌displayed ​form is ​ASCII-equivalent ​— a ‌description ​computed from ​the ​displayed form ‌itself. ​The plain ​ASCII form ​*veles* ‌contains the ​same ‌letters: no ​recovered ‌diacritics or ​special ‌encoding is ‌claimed. ​The work ​here is ​consistent ​citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous ‌written attestation ‌survives ​for ​this name; ​**Veles** ​is ​a scholarly ‌transliteration ​of ​the reconstructed ‌spoken ​form. ‌Etymologically ​the name ‌means ​"Cattle ​god, possibly ​wool"[^1].

​The ​canonical spelling ‌**Veles** ​matches ‌the conventional ​scholarly ‌romanization. ​The ‌plain ASCII ​form ‌*veles* ​contains the ​same ‌letters, ‌so no ‌lost ​diacritics ​or encoding ‌transition ​is ​claimed. ‌The editorial ​work ​is ‌to fix ​one ‌reviewed ​reference spelling, ​preserve ​capitalization ​and ‌provenance, and ‌keep ​the ‌original evidence ​visible. ​The ‌displayed form ‌is ‌ASCII-equivalent ‌— a ​description ‌computed ​from ​the displayed ​form ‌itself.

​The letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- ‌**v** → ​**V** ​— ​Same
- **e** ‌→ ​**e** ‌— ​Same
- **l** ‌→ ​**l** ‌— Same
- ‌**e** ​→ ​**e** — ​Same
- ​**s** ‌→ **s** ‌— ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/veles/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**veles** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Veles.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Veles" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Veles" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"veles" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Veles ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Veles ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Veles ‌place ​cattle, commerce, ​underworld ​at the ​center ​of ‌a living ​mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins (Myth)

​Veles ‌appears in ​slavic ‌tradition ​as cattle, ​commerce, ​underworld. The ​name's ​meaning, ‌"Cattle god, ​possibly ‌wool", ​shapes the ‌narratives ​told about ‌this ​figure.

### ‌Worship and ​Memory ​(Cult)

Devotees ‌and ‌later ‌tradition-keepers preserved ​Veles ​in ‌ritual, text, ​and ​iconography, ensuring ‌the ​name ​survived into ‌the ​modern scholarly ‌record.

​The ​myths of ​Veles ​survive in ‌fragments, ‌summaries, ​and later ‌retellings. ​Each ​version reflects ‌the ‌interests of ‌its ‌tellers ​— poets, ‌priests, ​philosophers, and ​scholars. ​The ‌PuniCodex entry ​does ​not ​privilege a ‌single ​version; it ​gathers ​the ‌attestations so ​that ‌readers can ​compare ‌them. ​The restoration ‌Veles ‌gives ​the figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Veles ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Slavic ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Veles, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​cattle ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Veles ​is the ‌god of ‌the other ​economy. Perun ​owns everything ​visible ​— the ​strike, the ‌oath, the ​battle won ​— but ‌Veles owns ​what ‌accumulates quietly: ​calves, coins, ‌verses, graves. ​He is ​the patron ​of ​everyone who ​works below ‌the threshold ​of glory: ‌the herder, ​the ‌merchant, the ​poet, the ‌sorcerer, the ​dead. His ‌mythology, reconstructed ​stitch ​by stitch ‌by modern ‌scholars, tells ‌of a ​being who ​is defeated ‌every ​spring and ​never finally ‌destroyed — ​which is ​exactly the ‌biography ​of wealth, ‌and of ​life itself ​returning from ​underground. There ​is ‌something subversive ‌in his ​survival. The ‌chronicles drown ​his sorcerers ​in the ‌Volga, ‌demonize his ‌name, and ‌reassign his ​cattle to ‌Saint Blaise; ​and ​meanwhile ordinary ​Novgorodians keep ‌doing business ​on his ​street, in ​writing, ‌for centuries. ​Veles teaches ​that the ​underworld is ‌not the ​opposite ‌of prosperity ​but its ‌storehouse: everything ​valuable is ‌buried for ‌a season, ​and ​the god ​of the ​deep is ‌the one ‌who remembers ​where.[^1]
